newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sterling main concern for Ireland after EMU-C.Bank.
newsitem.headline: Sterling main concern for Ireland after EMU-C.Bank.

text.p: Irish central bank governor Maurice O'Connell said on Thursday that while EMU was a "great vision" it was likely to be a mixed blessing for Ireland, with the behaviour of sterling the main concern.
O'Connell said each particular country had its own set of difficulties, and the focus in Ireland was almost exclusively on sterling, particularly if Britain stayed out of EMU and Ireland went in.
"The question is -- how will sterling behave outside EMU? We really don't know," O'Connell said a conference hosted by the irish Business and Employers' Confederation (IBEC).

O'Connell said sterling had historically demonstrated a great capacity to be erratic, and because of its track record over the past three decades, "it is reasonable to feel that it will be erratic in future."
Contrary to many predictions, sterling appreciated by 20 percent against the mark in the last year.
"This experience demonstrates that perhaps we need to consider the impact of an appreciating, as well as a depreciating sterling," he said.
O'Connell said a dominant issue at the moment was the rate at which currencies will be fixed in a single currency.
Speculation that Ireland will want the punt to enter EMU at its central Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) level of 2.41 marks has caused major sell-offs in the currency.
The Irish unit is currently trading close to 2.60 marks and there are fears of further speculative sell-offs of the currency over the next 18-months.

"Despite rumours, I can tell you that this issue (the rate currencies fix at) has not yet been considered by the appropriate authorities. It would be unwise to reach a conclusion on this so far in advance," O'Connell told delegates.
O'Connell said EMU was still 19 months away, and "19 months is quite a long time in market language".
The governor said preparations for EMU in the banking sector were well on course.
"As far as the central bank is concerned, all our business will be conducted in euro from day 1," he said.
O'Connell said a three and a half year transition period was too long and the possibility of introducing banknotes and coins some months ahead of the deadline of 2002 was being explored.

He said no matter how well countries analysed and prepared for EMU there was still an element of leaping into the dark. But, he added, he was more optimistic now about the general economic environment in Europe than one year ago.
